pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, citing their own NOTES.md output where the question asks for evidence; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: What does the Go memory model actually promise, and what is happens-before? List the operations you used in this exercise (and in S3) that create an edge — and name two things people assume create one but don't.
expected_points: a read is guaranteed to observe a write only if the write happens-before the read; within one goroutine program order gives that for free, across goroutines it must be established

edges: go f() before f's first statement; a send before the corresponding receive completes; close before a receive that returns the zero value; mu.Unlock before a later mu.Lock; wg.Done before Wait returning; once.Do's f returning before any Do returns; an atomic Load that observes an atomic Store
non-edges: a goroutine simply exiting, time.Sleep or any amount of waiting, and 'the write is one machine word so it must be visible'
the edge carries everything done before it, not just the synchronized variable — that is why Unlock/Lock publishes the whole critical section

questions.prompt: Take the lesson's `ready`/`conn` lazy-init snippet, or the starter's `Store`. Show me the race, and explain why the memory model calls the program undefined rather than just 'sometimes stale'. How did you fix `Store`, and why is that fix enough?
expected_points: two goroutines access the same location, at least one writing, with no happens-before edge between them — that is the definition, independent of timing

consequences are not limited to staleness: writes may be reordered (ready true while conn is nil), the compiler may hoist the read out of a loop and never re-read, and multi-word values like strings/slices/interfaces can tear
the memory model gives racy programs no defined behavior at all, so 'benign race' is not a category

the fix names the invariant first: Store publishes one immutable pointer, so atomic.Pointer[Config] Store/Load creates the edge (a mutex would also work; sync.Once/OnceValue is the equivalent fix for the lazy-init version)
the edge makes the pointed-to Config's fields visible too — which requires that published Configs are never mutated afterwards

questions.prompt: Why did `Meter` need a mutex when `Store` could use an atomic? What would go wrong with `atomic.Int64` for `hits` plus `atomic.Value` for `last`?
expected_points: Meter's two fields form one invariant: a Snapshot must describe a single moment
per-field atomics keep each field individually intact but let Snapshot pair a new count with an old event, or a positive count with an empty last — atomicity composes only over one word
Store's whole state is one pointer to an immutable value, which is exactly the single-word publication case atomics exist for
the general rule: the synchronization must span the invariant, not the variable; mutex is the default, atomics are the special case

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between stack and heap allocation in Go, and why you can't choose. What makes a value escape, and does taking its address force it onto the heap?
expected_points: stack allocation is a pointer bump freed by returning from the function and invisible to the GC; heap objects are shared, outlive frames, and cost the collector work (last lesson's bill)
Go has no allocate-on-the-heap keyword — new, &T{} and var all just create values; the compiler's escape analysis proves whether a value can outlive its frame
taking an address does not force the heap: if the value provably dies with the frame it stays on the stack

typical escape causes: returned by pointer, stored in something heap-reachable (slice/map/field/global/channel), captured by an outliving closure, boxed into an interface such as fmt's ...any, or too big/dynamically sized
escaping is a cost question, not a correctness question — sometimes the API requires it

questions.prompt: Walk me through your NOTES.md 'before' output. What command produced it, why does it need `-a`, and what do `escapes to heap`, `does not escape` and `leaking param` each tell you?
expected_points: go build -a -gcflags='-m' . 2>&1, usually filtered to drop inlining chatter; -m=2 shows the reasoning chain
-a forces a full recompile so the diagnostics are guaranteed; the build cache normally replays them anyway, but a stale cache is the first thing to suspect when -m prints nothing
'escapes to heap' / 'moved to heap' means a real allocation at that site
'does not escape' means a pointer parameter provably stays within the callee, so callers keep it on the stack
'leaking param' means the function stores or returns the pointer it was given, so the caller's value may escape because of this call
cites their own lines: &Report{} escaping because SummarizeHeap returns it by pointer, and format.go's 'value escapes to heap' from boxing into fmt's ...any

questions.prompt: For `AppendSample` and `Summarize`: what was the escaping value, what did you change, and what evidence proves it worked? Why does this lesson gate on allocation counts instead of timings?
expected_points: AppendSample: every fmt argument was boxed into ...any and Sprintf built a fresh string; rebuilt with append plus strconv.AppendInt so digits go straight into the caller's buffer — zero allocations when dst has capacity
Summarize: returning *Report forced the value to outlive the frame; returning the Report by value keeps it in the caller's frame and nothing escapes
evidence is twofold: the escape-analysis lines disappear from the -m output, and testing.AllocsPerRun / -benchmem show allocs/op drop to 0 (versus 1 for SummarizeHeap)

allocation counts are deterministic and identical under -race, on a laptop or in CI; ns/op varies with the machine and is distorted several-fold by the race detector, so benchmarks here are read by hand and never asserted on
the append-into-a-caller-owned-buffer pattern is the standard library's own (strconv.AppendInt, Time.AppendFormat)

questions.prompt: The race tests failed on your very first `-race` run rather than intermittently. Why? And what does a clean `-race` run NOT prove?
expected_points: the detector tracks the happens-before graph of the execution (vector clocks), not timing coincidences — if two unsynchronized accesses to the same address both execute and at least one writes, it reports
so it does not need the two accesses to land at the same nanosecond — races on executed paths are found reliably rather than by luck, which is why -race in CI is a gate worth having
it is still not a proof of absence: it only sees accesses that execute, and its per-address history is bounded, so a race can slip past even on a path that ran
what it never does is report a race that is not there — a report is evidence, a clean run is only the absence of evidence
cost is 2-20x time and extra memory, so the schedule you observe under -race is not the production schedule — another reason never to assert wall-clock behavior

questions.prompt: `Summarize` returns a 32-byte struct by value while `SummarizeHeap` returns an 8-byte pointer — the pointer moves fewer bytes. Why is the value version cheaper anyway, and when would returning a pointer be the right design?
expected_points: the copy is a few stack writes; the pointer version costs an allocation now plus mark-and-sweep work later, which the last lesson quantified
bytes copied is the wrong metric — allocations and GC pressure are the metric
pointer returns earn their keep for large structs, values the caller must mutate in place, shared identity, or when nil is a meaningful result
the alternative escape hatch is the append/writer shape: let the caller own the memory (AppendSample, io.Writer) so the API stops deciding to allocate
